standard.title: Identify source origin and purpose
standard.description: identify the origin, content, context and purpose of primary and secondary sources
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can evaluate primary and secondary sources to determine origin, purpose, and perspectives (AC9HS6S04). They have not yet applied these skills specifically to historical sources in the context of historical inquiry — distinguishing origin, content, context, and purpose as four distinct analytical dimensions, and applying disciplinary questions ('Who wrote/produced this?', 'When?', 'Why?', 'What does it show about the past?') systematically.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify and explain the origin, content, context, and purpose of primary and secondary sources by applying disciplinary analytical questions, demonstrating understanding of how each dimension contributes to interpreting what a source can and cannot tell us about the past.

nodes.label: Origin and content — the basic analytical questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the origin of a source (who produced it, when, and where) and describe its content (what it shows, says, or contains), applying the questions 'Who?', 'When?', 'What?'
nodes.minimum_width: For a given source, identify who produced it, when it was produced, and describe what it shows or contains.
nodes.typical_width: For a given primary or secondary source, systematically identify its origin — who produced it (individual, institution, group), when it was produced, and where — and describe its content — what it shows, depicts, records, or argues. Apply this to multiple source types (photographs, artefacts, texts, buildings).
wider: Examine cases where origin is difficult to establish — sources without clear attribution, ancient texts with disputed authorship, artefacts without provenance — and discuss what the difficulty of establishing origin means for interpreting the source.

Investigate how the origin of a source shapes its content — why an official court record contains certain types of information and omits others, why a personal letter reveals different things than a public inscription.

Explore the specific challenge of establishing origin for some ancient sources — such as the Kimberley Bradshaw paintings, where origin in terms of culture, period, and even subject matter remains debated.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate origin with content (or skip origin to jump to interpretation) will apply OCCP incompletely in N3 — context and purpose analysis requires a reliable origin/content foundation, and the synthesis node cannot integrate dimensions that haven't been clearly separated.

response_modes.reason: Systematic application of 'Who? When? What?' to diverse source types is a precision skill that requires practice across many examples. Students frequently conflate origin with content (what is shown vs who made it) or skip origin analysis to jump to interpretation. Regular practice across different source types — artefacts, photographs, texts, buildings — builds the reliable habit of beginning source analysis with origin and content before moving to context and purpose.

success_criteria: Correctly identifies the producer (who), period (when), and location (where) of a source's origin.
Accurately describes the content — what the source shows, contains, or records — without yet interpreting what it means.
Distinguishes origin from content — keeps the 'who made it' question separate from the 'what does it show' question.

nodes.label: Context and purpose — the interpretive questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the historical context in which a source was produced and identify its purpose — why it was made — and describe how context and purpose affect what a source reveals about the past.
nodes.minimum_width: For a given source, explain the historical context in which it was produced and identify its purpose (why it was made).
nodes.typical_width: For a given primary or secondary source, explain the historical context — the period, events, social conditions, and circumstances that surrounded its production — and identify its purpose: was it ceremonial, propagandistic, administrative, commemorative, communicative, artistic? Explain how the context and purpose shape what the source includes, excludes, and emphasises.
wider: Examine how political context shapes the purpose of sources — how rulers commissioned art, monuments, and texts for specific purposes (legitimation, propaganda, commemoration) — and what this means for reading them as historical evidence.

Investigate how the intended audience for a source shapes its content and purpose — a public inscription vs a private letter vs an official administrative record each have different audiences and therefore different purposes and omissions.

Explore how context and purpose interact in complex sources — a funerary text that is simultaneously religious, commemorative, administrative, and personal — and how identifying multiple purposes enriches source interpretation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate context with setting ('it's from Ancient Egypt') and purpose with content cannot produce integrated OCCP conclusions in N3 — the synthesis node requires all four dimensions to be clearly differentiated before they can be coordinated into an interpretive conclusion.

response_modes.reason: Context and purpose are more abstract than origin and content, and students frequently conflate them ('the context is Ancient Egypt' conflates setting with the specific circumstances of production; 'the purpose is to show X' conflates content with intent). The reasoning chain — who made this → for what audience → under what circumstances → with what intent → therefore it shows/omits X — needs explicit scaffolding before students can apply it reliably.

success_criteria: Correctly identifies the historical context of a source's production — not just 'it's from ancient times' but specific circumstances.
Identifies the purpose of the source — ceremonial, propagandistic, administrative, commemorative — with reasoning.
Explains how context and purpose affect what the source reveals and what it omits.

nodes.label: Integrating OCCP — what can this source tell us?
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can integrate origin, content, context, and purpose analysis to explain what a source can and cannot tell us about the past, and apply this analytical framework to sources from the Deep Time and Ancient units.
nodes.minimum_width: For a given source, apply all four analytical dimensions (origin, content, context, purpose) and draw a conclusion about what the source can tell us about a specific historical question.
nodes.typical_width: For a primary or secondary source from the History Y7 units, systematically apply origin, content, context, and purpose analysis and synthesise the four dimensions into a conclusion about what the source can tell us, what it cannot tell us, and why. Apply to source types from both the Deep Time unit (artefacts, oral tradition, rock art) and the Ancient unit (inscriptions, artefacts, artworks, historical texts).
wider: Apply the OCCP framework to a source that is challenging or ambiguous — such as the Kimberley Bradshaw paintings (disputed origin), ancient oral traditions (uncertain authorship and transmission), or propaganda inscriptions (purpose that complicates reliability) — and explain how the challenge affects what can be concluded.
Compare OCCP analysis of two sources about the same event or person, examining how different origins and purposes produce different accounts and what a historian can conclude from the comparison.
Examine how the OCCP framework connects to the broader historical skill of corroboration — why multiple sources analysed through OCCP produce more reliable interpretations than any single source.

response_modes.reason: This node integrates origin/content (Node 1) and context/purpose (Node 2) into the descriptor's full demand — applying all four analytical dimensions together to reach a conclusion about what a source can and cannot tell us. Students must coordinate the four dimensions, not treat them as separate boxes to fill in, and synthesise them into an interpretive conclusion.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The application of OCCP analysis to challenging sources — oral traditions, rock art, propaganda, disputed attributions — is inherently rich and raises methodological questions about what counts as historical evidence. Advancing students can engage with how historians handle sources with disputed origins or complex purposes, and develop the understanding that source analysis is interpretive work, not a mechanical checklist. The comparison of OCCP analyses across multiple sources also builds the corroboration skill central to historical reasoning.
success_criteria: Applies all four dimensions (origin, content, context, purpose) to a source systematically.
Draws a reasoned conclusion about what the source can and cannot tell us about a specific historical question.
Does not treat OCCP as four separate boxes — synthesises the dimensions into an integrated interpretive conclusion.
